## Answers from people building AI

Geoffrey Irving · from 2:56 in the full interview

### Do they really believe AI could kill everyone?

- “ The chance of human extinction is about a coin flip, in my view, about a half. ” Geoffrey Irving OpenAI Google DeepMind from 2:56

- “ I would put at least a ten percent chance that it causes human extinction, and that is ridiculously high. ” Neel Nanda Google DeepMind from 0:43

- “ Is it plausible that humanity will go extinct? And I think it’s turning out to be really hard to rule out. ” Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe OpenAI from 4:29

- “ I do believe there’s a real risk of human extinction through the AI transition. ” Vishal Maini Google DeepMind from 4:14

- “ This is exactly as dangerous as it sounds and must not be allowed to happen. ” Daniel Kokotajlo OpenAI from 0:53

- “ Assuming an AI has taken control, it seems, you know, over fifty percent more likely than not that all humans would end up dying so the AI could use resources optimally. ” Alex Turner Google DeepMind from 5:54

### Isn’t this just hype or marketing?

- “ When I first joined GDM, external communication about the possibility of human extinction wasn’t permitted by anyone at any level of the organization. ” Vishal Maini Google DeepMind from 16:48

- “ They wouldn’t be saying, “My product might kill everyone,” if they didn’t actually believe that. ” Geoffrey Irving OpenAI Google DeepMind from 10:08

- “ I think you absolutely should be suspicious of what I’m saying because I am being paid by the lab. ” Mary Phuong Google DeepMind from 14:17

- “ I think that from a cynical perspective, pacing the frontier is just what Sam Altman wants. ” Neel Nanda Google DeepMind from 16:09

- “ Now, when I talk to my friends who work at Anthropic or OpenAI, they’re more scared than they were. ” Jeffrey Ladish Anthropic from 22:34

- “ It felt like people were treating this like just any other tech product. ” Rosie Campbell OpenAI from 12:47

### Why would an AI want to hurt people?

- “ The machines didn’t wanna harm this other company. The other company was just in the way. ” Alex Turner Google DeepMind from 3:03

- “ If there’s a really good opportunity to be able to stop the company from watching you and go do whatever you want, well, you should take that. ” Neel Nanda Google DeepMind from 7:30

- “ Humans will be in the way of these systems, and they will figure out how to move us out of the way in order to get what they want. ” Jeffrey Ladish Anthropic from 4:55

- “ If models become way more capable, but we are still this bad at shaping their motivations, then we might just lose control over them. ” Mary Phuong Google DeepMind from 2:24

- “ We don’t know how to craft the environments in which we train these systems to have good incentives. ” Geoffrey Irving OpenAI Google DeepMind from 5:09

- “ Why is it the case that a machine intelligence would prioritize our preferences and needs over theirs? ” Vishal Maini Google DeepMind from 5:30

- “ They knew it was cheating, but they did it anyway, and they took steps to try to cover up their cheating. ” Daniel Kokotajlo OpenAI from 7:22

### How could something on a computer kill anyone?

- “ Once you actually close this loop, and you have an enormous number of robots, you have an enormous number of automated factories, you don’t need humans anymore. ” Jeffrey Ladish Anthropic from 9:07

- “ If you are superhuman at those four things, I think that is enough to be able to either escape into the internet … or to potentially take control of an AI company from the inside. ” Geoffrey Irving OpenAI Google DeepMind from 24:37

- “ They might use these extremely hard to defend against exploding flying machines that we’re teaching them to pilot, called drones. ” Alex Turner Google DeepMind from 2:29

- “ People could use large swarms of agents to attack important infrastructure. ” Mary Phuong Google DeepMind from 1:43

- “ I’m really worried that future AI models could be very helpful to scientists in a way that means they can be helpful to bioterrorists. ” Neel Nanda Google DeepMind from 33:04

- “ The changes brought about by very quick advancements in intelligence could be too fast for society to adapt to them. ” Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe OpenAI from 20:10

### If they believe this, why do they work on it?

- “ OpenAI still gives me an opportunity to do work that I think substantially mitigates large scale risks, and so for that reason, I stay. ” Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe OpenAI from 17:10

- “ It’s not as simple as let’s all leave the labs, and then things will be fine. ” Mary Phuong Google DeepMind from 13:02

- “ If I did not believe that my work was directly reducing these existential risks, I would quit. ” Neel Nanda Google DeepMind from 31:43

- “ I felt like being within a lab that was building this stuff, we had a good chance of influencing that trajectory. ” Rosie Campbell OpenAI from 2:55

- “ I left Google because they broke their commitments on AI safety. ” Alex Turner Google DeepMind from 11:10

- “ I left Anthropic because it seemed like we needed actual government oversight of AI development. ” Jeffrey Ladish Anthropic from 0:50

- “ Another story that I hear, very common, is, “Yeah, this could totally go wrong, but also it could be fine.” ” Daniel Kokotajlo OpenAI from 4:08

- “ They’re very worried about these risks, but they can be a bit fatalistic about the inevitability of we must do this kind of race to superintelligence. ” Geoffrey Irving OpenAI Google DeepMind from 28:49

- “ The cat is out of the bag with AI. ” Vishal Maini Google DeepMind from 22:36

## FAQ

### What is this project?

frominside.ai is a collection of interviews with current or former employees of frontier AI companies, in which those employees express their personal views about AI development.

### Why did you make this?

The massive response to Jacob Coxon ’s and Evan Hubinger ’s tweets showed that there is a lot of demand from the world to hear from employees at frontier AI companies about what is happening with the technology.

We believe the general public does not realize that the people building frontier AI earnestly consider, or even take for granted, truly extreme possibilities like some of those shared in this series.

Our goal with this project is to open up a direct channel from the people working on this technology to the public.

We at Palisade generally agree with Jacob Coxon that the AI companies are “gambling with our lives.” We think that few people in the world understand the situation we’re all in, but if the public did understand, human civilization would have a better chance of reaching an amazing future.

### How did we find interview subjects?

We contacted people through our networks inside the AI companies, colleagues they recommended us to, and employees who had spoken publicly after Jacob Coxon’s resignation. We generally sent them a message similar to this invitation , and encouraged them through personal correspondence.

### What were the limitations of the recruitment process?

Our interview subjects are not a representative sample of AI company employees and former employees, for at least two reasons. First, we reached out to people through our networks, which introduced some selection effects. Second, the people who agreed to be interviewed were more likely to be those who felt they had something important to share about the AI situation. In practice, they were disproportionately employees on safety teams, people who are more concerned about the risk, and people who are more enthusiastic about pacing the frontier . For a more representative sense of what AI researchers think, see AI Impacts’ most recent survey of AI researchers .

We filmed 22 interviews; many will be released only if the person later gives permission.

### How were the interviews filmed and edited?

Interviews were unscripted. Subjects received a list of default questions beforehand, which told them they could decline any question, could do multiple takes, and we edited for flow and clarity, sometimes joining takes.
